posts.title: A black hole jet moves at near-light speed but barely shifts across the sky
posts.description: Black holes can launch matter into space at nearly the speed of light, but how these enormous jets form, accelerate, and change direction remains a major astrophysical mystery. Now, astronomers have used the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) to observe a black hole’s jet that appears to bend toward Earth within a fraction of a parsec. The discovery could explain why some parts of these outflows appear unusually bright while moving more slowly across the sky, Closer look at black hole’s jet The object behind the discovery is 3C 279, a blazar in the constellation Virgo. It hosts a supermassive black hole with an estimated mass of 800 million Suns, which powers a jet of electrically charged particles moving at relativistic speeds. Blazars are useful for studying these outflows because their jets point almost directly toward Earth. This orientation makes them appear exceptionally bright through relativistic beaming. posts.title: 10 unusual ways to generate electricity that engineers have put to the test
posts.description: Most electricity comes from familiar machinery. Steam spins turbines in power plants, wind turns blades, and solar cells convert sunlight into electricity. But those machines tap only a fraction of the places where energy changes hands. Every footstep pushes against the ground. A rooftop loses heat after sunset. Even two streams of water with different salt concentrations can drive a turbine. Engineers are finding ways to capture that energy. Some of their devices already feed electricity into the grid. Others produce just enough to light an LED or run a computer chip. 1. Flying underwater kites in tidal currents In the Faroe Islands, a tethered kite flies in a figure-eight pattern beneath the surface. The current pushes against its wing, and the kite’s looping path lets it travel faster than the water around it. posts.title: US Navy’s amphibious assault ship deploys armored vehicles aboard LCAC hovercraft
posts.description: The U.S. Navy has released new images showing one of its most versatile amphibious transport systems in action. The photos capture three Marine Corps LAV-25 armored reconnaissance vehicles riding aboard a Landing Craft Air Cushion (LCAC) as it launched from the amphibious assault ship USS Boxer during operations in the Middle East. The exercise shows how the Navy and Marine Corps can get their troops, their tanks, and their heavy equipment from the ship onto the shore very quickly, indeed without the need for ports or docks. The hovercraft can just zip across the open sea and then hover over the beach, the mudflats and all the other sorts of terrain that would stop a conventional landing craft.
